newsitem.title: USA: SEC takes action in Arizona county bond probe.
newsitem.headline: SEC takes action in Arizona county bond probe.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission said Monday it brought precedent-setting enforcement action against Maricopa County, Ariz., following a two-year probe of the county's municipal bond deals.

The SEC alleged that the county violated the anti-fraud provisions of federal securities laws in connection with the July 1993 sale of two series of general obligation bonds by failing to disclose a worsening of the county's finances.

In a statement issued by the SEC's Los Angeles office, the commission said it instituted cease and desist proceedings against the Arizona county, the sixth largest county in the nation. The county includes the city of Phoenix.

The SEC action against Maricopa County was precedent setting, according to Paul Maco, director of SEC's Office of Municipal Securities in Washington. It was the first action by the commission against a general purpose issuer of municipal bonds where the securities were not in default.
Following the SEC annoucement, the county said in a statement that its Board of Supervisors would meet on Oct. 2 to consider an offer to settle with the SEC.
In settling, the county said it would neither admit nor deny any of the SEC's allegations. In addition, no fines or penalties would be imposed on the county.
"There is nothing to gain, from the county's perspective, by engaging in protracted litigation now over events that occurred over three years ago," the county said.
The official statements for the Maricopa County bond offerings contained financial information about the county for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1992.

The SEC said, however, that the county's financial condition at the time of the offerings had worsened. The county had developed a deficit in its general fund. The SEC said the county's cash flow position had also declined.
The SEC alleged the official statements for the bonds failed to disclose these developments.

In addition, the SEC said the official statement for one of the offerings represented that the bond proceeds were to be used to finance specific county projects. The county used the money, however, to finance its deficit, the SEC alleged.

"Each of the omitted items referenced above would have been important for an investor to consider in deciding whether or not to purchase the county's bonds because they tended to bear upon the county's financial condition at the time the bonds were issued," the SEC said.
In its statement, the county said the financial problems that it faced in 1993 have been addressed.
"The prospects for a healthy financial future for Maricopa County are bright and attainable," the county said.
The SEC declined to comment on whether its investigation of the county bond deals would continue and whether the probe would now focus on municipal bond professionals.
